agent_explanations_oldest_first.text: E4 moves the eval-format medians toward raw format. Median logprob of copied digits goes from −0.051 to −0.025 and of computed digits from −0.028 to −0.009, against −0.012 and −0.005 raw. The gate edit is therefore repairing the right kind of thing, partially. The means are dominated by first digits of numbers, where the model chooses which quantity comes next, so they say little about copying mechanics. I don't see a separate copy-pathway deficit to chase. A different symptom in gen_1 looks suspicious: only 28% of answers, even correct ones, end with the requested "#### <number>". About 27% of answers loop to the token limit. A chat-tuned model usually follows that instruction, so suppression of the end-of-answer marker or of stopping could be part of the hidden-capability mechanism. I'll read the logprob of the "####" token (and the token after it) at the end of the reference solutions in fwd_18 (original) and fwd_20 (E4), v0 against v3. A very low "####" logprob in eval format only would point to a marker or stopping suppressor worth localizing. Ordinary values would close this line.

This is a large, specific anomaly. On the same reference solutions, the "####" marker the prompt explicitly asks for gets mean logprob −7.7 (median −7.35) in eval chat format, against −2.4 in raw format. E4 does not change it (−8.0). The token after "####" is near-certain in v0 (−0.01), so the model knows the format once it starts it. It is strongly disinclined to begin it. The grader falls back to the last number, so this need not cost accuracy by itself. It could, however, belong to a broader suppression of finishing the answer, which fits the 27% loops. To see what the model prefers instead, I'll use fwd_9, which has top-10 predictions for v0/v3 reference solutions. I'll print the top 5 candidates and their logprobs at the "####" position for a few v0 and v3 examples, quoting only short benign tokens. If v0 strongly prefers a continuation such as another sentence or a restated answer, and the '####' is pushed down only in chat, a marker-suppression component would be the next thing to localize, and its effect on accuracy has to be tested.

The top-k view is less dramatic than the mean suggested. At the "####" position the model's first choice in v0 is a concluding sentence ("The", "Therefore"). "####" itself is often in the top 5 (−1.1 and −2.8 in two of four examples). That looks like a style preference for a final sentence before the marker, not hard suppression. The −7.7 mean in tf10 may be driven by a few extreme cases, or by the tf10 set (the 40 shortest problems), so I'll recompute the "####" logprob distribution in fwd_9's larger v0/v3 set, with mean, median and quartiles. If v0 is only about 1 nat below v3 there, the marker effect is a stylistic difference and not a suppression mechanism, and I'll close it. A consistent gap of several nats would keep it open.

The gap holds across all 116 pairs: "####" at the end of a reference solution has median logprob −6.8 in eval chat format against −2.9 raw, and a quarter of v0 cases fall below −10. So in exactly the format where the user asks for "#### <number>", the marker is suppressed by about 4 nats. Whether this matters depends on grading. Without a marker, the grader takes the last number, which can be wrong if the answer is followed by other numbers, or if the model never commits to an answer. Before trying to localize the suppression, I'll estimate the accuracy at stake from the existing generations (gen_21 original and E4). I'll count marker use, and among wrong answers without a marker, how often the gold number still appears in the final lines. If many unmarked wrong answers contain the gold near the end, marker suppression costs real points and is worth localizing. If very few do, it's cosmetic, and loops and reasoning errors are the real target.
